Task 2

Now we will use the lm method on the dowsing data to generate the following plot:

# Generate plot
dowsing |> ggplot(aes(x = GUESS, y= PIPE)) +
    geom_point(colour = "navy") +
      stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y~x)

The regression line equation can be represented as follows:

# Get lm model and summary
mod <- lm(PIPE~GUESS, data = dowsing)

summary(mod)

Task 3

Now we can assess the model assumptions.

Part a

Here we will assess the assumption that \(\epsilon_i \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) by plotting the residuals vs fitted-values:

# Get residuals
res <- residuals(mod)

# Get fitted values
fitval <- fitted.values(mod)

# Generate the plot with the loess line
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = fitval, y = res)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 0, col = "red", lty = 2) +
    geom_point(colour = "navy") +
      stat_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y~x) + 
        labs(title = "Residuals vs. Fitted")

From this diagnostic plot I can see a distinct non-linear pattern in the residuals across fitted-values as indicated by the LOESS line. Additionally the residuals appear to not be uniformly dispersed around the \(0\) center line which would indicate non-equal variances across fitted-values. Therefore, I would proceed with caution since the assumptions of homoscedasticity and linearity are likely violated.

Part b

Now we can check the assumption that the residuals are normally distributed:

# Assess normality
s20x::normcheck(mod, shapiro.wilk = TRUE)

Part c

The QQ-Plot indicates that our residuals fall close to the theoretical quantities if normally distributed and that the Shapiro-Wilk test indicates that we fail to reject \(H_0\), which states the residuals are normally distributed, at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level (\(W = 0.9869\), \(p = 0.978\)). Additionally the histogram of our residuals indicates a fairly normal distribution. Therefore these results support the assumption of normality is not violated.

Task 4

Here we will make the required function:

# Define function
myciplot <- function(lm_mod, alpha = 0.05, f = 2/3){
  
  # Get useful values
  res <- residuals(lm_mod)
  fitval <- fitted.values(lm_mod)
  
  # Get summary of your linear model
  sm <- summary(lm_mod)
  
  # Get ci for beta parameters
  ci <- confint(lm_mod, level = 1-alpha)
  
  # Define estimates for beta0, beta1 and sigma2
  hbeta0 <- sm$coefficients[1,1]
  hbeta1 <- sm$coefficients[2,1]
  hsigma2 <- sm$sigma**2
  
  # Define the 100(1-alpha)% ci for each parameter above
  beta0_ci <- ci[1,]
  beta1_ci <- ci[2,]
  low_sig <- paste0(alpha/2 *100, "%") 
  high_sig <- paste0((1-alpha/2)*100, "%")
  sigma2_ci <- setNames( c((sm$df[2]*hsigma2 / qchisq(1-alpha/2, sm$df[2])), 
                          (sm$df[2]*hsigma2 / qchisq(alpha/2, sm$df[2]))), 
                         c(low_sig, high_sig))
  
  # Histogram of residuals
  h <- hist(res, plot = FALSE)
  hcol <- h$density / max(h$density)
  
  hist(res,
       freq = FALSE,
       col = rgb(hcol, hcol^2, 0),
       xlab = "Residuals",
       ylab = "Density",
       main = "Distribution of Residuals")
  curve(dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = sm$sigma), col = "green", add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
  
  # Diagnostic plot
 
  plot(x = fitval, y = res,
       pch = 21,
       cex = 1.5,
       col = "black",
       bg = "green",
       main = "Diagnostic Plot",
       ylab = "Residuals",
       xlab = "Fitted Values",
       panel.first = {grid(col = "lightgray", lty = "dotted")
         abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)})
  lines(lowess(x = fitval, y = res, f = f), lwd = 2, col = "blue")
 
  
  # Output list
  out <- list(hbeta0 = hbeta0,
              hbeta1 = hbeta1,
              hsigma2 = hsigma2,
              beta0_ci = beta0_ci,
              beta1_ci = beta1_ci,
              sigma2_ci = sigma2_ci,
              residuals = res,
              fitted_values = fitval)
  
  return(invisible(out))
  
}

Task 5

To answer the question of “Can Dowsers actually detect water” we first need to define our hypotheses and describe exactly what they mean.

The hypotheses for our Simple Linear Regression (SLR) model are:

\[H_0: \beta_1 =0 \\ H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0\]

This is in general terms an assessment of the utility of the regression model that we come up with. What is meant by this is that does our independent variable contribute any useful information to the prediction of our dependent variable. By looking at the slope of our regression line \(\beta_1\) we can make this assessment. If our independent variable truly contributed no useful information to the prediction of our dependent variable then the slope \(\beta_1\) would equal \(0\). Conversely, If our independent variable did contributed useful information to the prediction of our dependent variable then the slope \(\beta_1\) would not equal \(0\).

The analysis of this hypothesis test for the DOWSING data can be seen below:

Analysis

First lets get the summary data:

# Model summary
summary(mod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = PIPE ~ GUESS, data = dowsing)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -51.858 -17.642  -0.083  15.856  49.841 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  
## (Intercept)  30.0737    11.4139   2.635   0.0145 *
## GUESS         0.3079     0.1900   1.620   0.1182  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 26.03 on 24 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.09861,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.06105 
## F-statistic: 2.626 on 1 and 24 DF,  p-value: 0.1182
# Confidence intervals
confint(mod, level = 0.95)
##                   2.5 %     97.5 %
## (Intercept)  6.51647453 53.6309116
## GUESS       -0.08427417  0.6999993

CI and Null Value

The output results indicate that the confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is \((-0.08427417, 0.6999993)\) at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level. We can see that this interval does include the null value of \(0\) and therefore it is a plausible slope and we fail to reject \(H_0\). Additionally this means that for every \(1\) meter increase in the Dowser’s guess of the pipelines location we’re not sure if its actual location increases or decreases relative to the guess.

P-value at \(\alpha = 0.05\)

The p-value for the slope \(\beta_1\) is \(0.1182\). Since \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(0.1182 > \alpha\) this means that we fail to reject \(H_0\) since our p-value is greater than our defined significance level.

RAR and \(T_{Calc}\)

For \(\beta_1\) we have \(T_{Calc} = 1.620\) as indicated from the model summary and now all we need to do is get our cut-off quantiles for the rejection/acceptance regions:

# Get quantiles for RAR - df = 24 from summary output
alpha = 0.05
lower <- qt(alpha/2, df = 24)
upper <- qt(1-alpha/2, df = 24)

# Output quantiles
lower
## [1] -2.063899
upper
## [1] 2.063899

As we can see our \(T_{Calc}= 1.620\) is within the acceptance region which lies between \(-2.063899\) and \(2.063899\). Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\) since \(T_{Calc}\) does not lie within the rejection regions.

Piecewise Regression

First lets read in the SPRUCE data:

# Read in data
spruce <- readxl::read_xls("~/Desktop/OU_Masters/Summer_2026/MATH-4753G_Summer_2026/K25936_Downloads/K25936_Downloads/Excel/SPRUCE.XLS")

Task 6

Now we can define the function that will aid us in finding the optimal \(R^2\) value for our change point:

# Define function
myknot <- function(x_k, x, y){
  
  # Get the adjustment term
  a <- (x - x_k)*(x>x_k)
  
  # Get the model
  mod <- lm(y ~ x + a)
  
  # Get r2
  out <- summary(mod)$r.squared
  
  # Return value
  return(out)
  
}

Next we will find the optimal \(x_k\) value to be our change point that maximizes \(R^2\):

# Get optimal x_k
opk <- optimise(myknot, interval = c(10,20), x = spruce$BHDiameter, y = spruce$Height, maximum = TRUE)

# Show result
opk
## $maximum
## [1] 17.44166
## 
## $objective
## [1] 0.7705864

From here we can generate a plot of the piecewise regression and the plot of \(R^2\) vs. \(x_k\):

# Fit piecewise model
pcw <- lm(Height ~ BHDiameter + I((BHDiameter-opk[[1]])*(BHDiameter>opk[[1]])), data = spruce) 

# Get coefficients
coeffs <- coef(pcw)

# Define the piecewise regression line for curve()
pcwf <- function(x, coeff, xk){
  
  coeff[[1]] + coeff[[2]]*(x) + coeff[[3]]*(x-xk)*(x-xk>0)
  
}

# Piecewise regression plot
plot(x = spruce$BHDiameter, y = spruce$Height,
     pch = 21,
     cex = 1.5,
     col = "black",
     bg = "green",
     main = "Height vs BHDiameter Piecewise Regression",
     ylab = "Height",
     xlab = "BHDiameter")
curve(pcwf(x, coeffs, opk[[1]]), add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 2)

# R2 vs x_k plot with abline at optimal x_k
x_k_seq <- seq(min(spruce$BHDiameter),max(spruce$BHDiameter), length = 1000)

R2s <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(x_k_seq))
for(i in 1:length(x_k_seq)){
  
  R2s[i] <- myknot(x_k_seq[i], x = spruce$BHDiameter, y = spruce$Height)
  
}

plot(x = x_k_seq, y = R2s, 
     type = "l", 
     col = "red",
     ylab = bquote(R^2),
     xlab = bquote(x[k]),
     main = bquote(bold(R^2 ~ "vs." ~ x[k])))
abline(v = opk[[1]], lwd = 2)

To make all of this more efficient we can combine all of these parts into one function:

# Combined Function - interval argument for root finding if you dont get the global maximum
mypiece_oneknot <- function(x, y, interval){
  
  # Nested function for optimal x_k finding
  myknot <- function(x_k, x, y){
    
    # Get the adjustment term
    a <- (x - x_k)*(x>x_k)
    
    # Get the model
    mod <- lm(y ~ x + a)
    
    # Get r2
    out <- summary(mod)$r.squared
    
    # Return value
    return(out)
    
  }
  
  
  # Get optimal x_k
  opk <- optimise(myknot, interval = interval, x = x, y = y, maximum = TRUE)
  
  # Fit piecewise model
  pcw <- lm(y ~ x + I((x-opk[[1]])*(x>opk[[1]]))) 
  
  # Get coefficients
  coeffs <- coef(pcw)
  
  # Define the piecewise regression line for curve()
  pcwf <- function(x, coeff, xk){
    
    coeff[[1]] + coeff[[2]]*(x) + coeff[[3]]*(x-xk)*(x-xk>0)
    
  }
  
  # Piecewise regression plot
  plot(x = x, y = y,
       pch = 21,
       cex = 1.5,
       col = "black",
       bg = "green",
       main = "Generalized Piecewise Regression - One Knot")
  curve(pcwf(x, coeffs, opk[[1]]), add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  
  # R2 vs x_k plot with abline at optimal x_k
  x_k_seq <- seq(min(x),max(x), length = 1000)
  
  R2s <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(x_k_seq))
  for(i in 1:length(x_k_seq)){
    
    R2s[i] <- myknot(x_k_seq[i], x = x, y = y)
    
  }
  
  plot(x = x_k_seq, y = R2s, 
       type = "l", 
       col = "red",
       ylab = bquote(R^2),
       xlab = bquote(x[k]),
       main = bquote(R^2 ~ "vs." ~ x[k]))
  abline(v = opk[[1]], lwd = 2)
  
  
  return(invisible(list(
    "Optimal x_k" = opk[[1]],
    "Optimized R Squared for Piecewise Model" = opk[[2]]
  )))
  
}

Test this combined function:

# Test function
results <- mypiece_oneknot(x = spruce$BHDiameter, y = spruce$Height, interval = c(5,30))

# Show output
results
## $`Optimal x_k`
## [1] 17.44165
## 
## $`Optimized R Squared for Piecewise Model`
## [1] 0.7705864
